book.title: Hip Fracture
book.lead: One of the most important fractures in older adults: early mobilisation saves function and lives.

blocks.text: Hip fracture means a fracture of the proximal femur: intracapsular (femoral neck) or extracapsular (intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric). Most occur in older adults after a fall from standing height. Hip fracture is associated with high mortality within a year and a large loss of independence [Ref – to verify]. Almost all are treated surgically: displaced intracapsular fractures with hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement; extracapsular fractures with screws, plates or nails. The aim is to allow full weight-bearing immediately after surgery in most patients [Ref – to verify].

blocks.label: WHY THIS MATTERS
body: Every day in bed increases the risk of pneumonia, blood clots, pressure ulcers, delirium and muscle loss. Getting the patient out of bed on the day after surgery is one of the most valuable things a physiotherapist does.

items: Fall, then hip or groin pain, inability to bear weight.
Leg shortened and externally rotated in displaced fractures.
Some impacted fractures allow walking with pain: be suspicious.

rows: What operation was performed? Any weight-bearing or movement restrictions?
How did you walk before the fall? Aids? Stairs? Living alone?
Why did you fall? Dizziness, blackout, trip?

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, tachycardia, low SpO2
Stop; lie the patient back; call medical emergency team
Systolic BP drop with dizziness or loss of consciousness
Return to bed, elevate legs, inform team
Leg shortening and rotation after movement
Do not move the leg; medical team

steps: **Day 0 to 1: check medical stability** (vital signs within agreed limits, Hb acceptable, no new chest pain).
**Stable:** sit out of bed and stand; walk with a frame if able.
**Unstable:** bed exercises and chest care; re-check later the same day.
**Progress daily:** distance, independence, stairs as needed, discharge planning.

blocks.text: Not a priority. Gentle soft-tissue work or assisted range only for comfort.

rows: Ankle pumps, static quadriceps and gluteal sets, deep breathing
Sit-to-stand from a raised chair, standing hip abduction and extension at the frame, mini-squats, walking with frame
Progress to stick, step-ups, stairs practice, heel raises
Progressive resistance training for hip extensors, abductors and quadriceps, balance training (Otago-style program), walking
2 to 3 times a week for months [Ref – to verify]

blocks.text: Hip precautions after hemiarthroplasty or replacement depend on surgical approach and local protocol. Many modern pathways use minimal precautions; follow the surgeon's instructions exactly.
Ice for swelling and pain; not essential. Compression stockings and anticoagulation are medical decisions.

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: An 82-year-old woman had a hemiarthroplasty yesterday for a displaced femoral neck fracture after tripping on a rug. She lived alone and walked with a stick. BP 118/70 lying, 96/60 sitting with dizziness. Hb slightly low.

blocks.text: > Plan: return to lying, inform the medical team about the orthostatic drop, bed exercises and breathing exercises, retry sitting later after fluids or review.

items: **Why mobilise on day 1?** To reduce complications and improve recovery of walking.
**What does her blood pressure drop mean?** Orthostatic hypotension, possibly from anaemia or fluid loss. Do not push standing; inform the team.
**What is the long-term exercise priority?** Progressive strength and balance training plus falls prevention.
**What else must be addressed before discharge?** Home hazards (rugs), aids, support, and bone health.
**Sudden breathlessness during walking?** Treat as possible pulmonary embolism: emergency.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Assess medical stability before mobilising a post-operative patient.
Recognise post-operative complications.
Plan early mobilisation and long-term strength and balance training.
